To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

macrophage cell death upon infection is not only dependent on the bacterial virulence factors and the macrophage immune responses, but also on the host genetic background and the macrophages’ metabolic status.

the macrophages infected by Francisella, Shigela, and Salmonella, but not by Yersinia, undergo cell death, which is a programmed cell death, and the cell death is induced by the bacteria, which are facultative intracellular pathogens.

the macrophage-pathogen interactions can be divided into two main categories, the first category is the pathogen-induced apoptosis, which is a form of programmed cell death (PCD), the second category is the non-programmed cell death (non-PCD) that is the pathogen induced pyroptosis, necroptotic cell death and necrosis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms of macrophage cell death upon bacterial infection, which will be useful for the development of new therapeutic strategies against bacterial infections.
understanding the molecular basis of macrophage cell death upon bacterial infection and the significance of macrophage-cell death in the context of host-pathogen interaction.
how the macrophages and bacteria interact with each other to achieve the final outcome of the battle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the outcome of the infection is dependent on the nature of the bacterial species and its virulence factors, as well as on the host cell and the host genetic background.
the macrophages can be killed by intracellular bacteria by a variety of different mechanisms.
the macrophages die by different ways depending on the bacterial species and the type of macrophage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
macrophages can kill bacteria by apoptosis and autophagy and bacteria can kill macrophages by necrosis and pyroptosis.

, in general, macrophages are more likely to die via apoptosis and autophagy upon infection by Francisella or Salmonella; whereas, macrophages die via necrosis upon Shigella and necroptosis upon Yersinia infection.

the outcome of macrophage-pathogen interaction depends on a number of factors, including the type of pathogens, the type of macrophages, the type of cell death, the cell death pathways, the type of death effector molecules and the cell death regulators.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the outcome of macrophage death is highly dependent on the type of pathogen and its virulence factors.
macrophage cell death can be induced by bacterial infection and this cell death may have a significant impact on bacterial infection.
the outcome of macrophage death upon bacterial infection is not only dependent on the type of macrophages, but also on the type and virulence of the bacteria, as well as the host environment.
